records.source: וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע בֶּן־שָׁא֗וּל כִּ֣י מֵ֤ת אַבְנֵר֙ בְּחֶבְר֔וֹן וַיִּרְפּ֖וּ יָדָ֑יו וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל נִבְהָֽלוּ׃
records.gloss: And heard [the] son of Saul that had died Abner in Hebron, and dropped his hands, and all Israel were dismayed.
pieces: When Saul's son heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost heart, and all Israel was alarmed.

L.1: And the son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, and his hands went slack, and all Israel was dismayed.

R.1: Saul's son Ish-bosheth heard that Abner had died in Hebron. Then he lost all his courage, and all the people of Israel were alarmed.

decisions.choice: the son of Saul: the Hebrew text does not give his name here
alternatives: Mephibosheth son of Saul (ancient Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "the son of Saul". The ancient Greek translation adds a name, calling him Mephibosheth, the name it uses for Ish-bosheth in this chapter. The man meant is Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, whom Abner had made king over Israel (2:8-10; 4:5). The Hebrew is followed; reviewers should check the Greek evidence.

decisions.choice: his hands dropped: his courage and strength failed
decisions.reason: Hands that hang limp picture a man who has lost the will to act (Isaiah 13:7; Jeremiah 6:24; Zephaniah 3:16).

decisions.choice: Abner's death left Ish-bosheth's kingdom without its real leader
decisions.reason: Abner had made Ish-bosheth king and held the power behind him (2:8-9; 3:6, 11). He had also begun to bring the northern tribes over to David (3:12-21) before Joab killed him at Hebron (3:27). "All Israel" is the kingdom of Ish-bosheth, set against Judah, as in chapter 2.

decisions.choice: Saul's son Ish-bosheth
decisions.reason: Readable names the son, as verse 5 does, so that a new reader knows who is meant.

decisions.choice: lost heart (Balanced); lost all his courage (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture of limp hands means. Literal keeps the picture.

records.heading: Ish-bosheth is murdered

records.source: וּשְׁנֵ֣י אֲנָשִׁ֣ים שָׂרֵֽי־גְדוּדִ֣ים הָי֪וּ בֶן־שָׁא֟וּל שֵׁם֩ הָאֶחָ֨ד בַּֽעֲנָ֜ה וְשֵׁ֧ם הַשֵּׁנִ֣י רֵכָ֗ב בְּנֵ֛י רִמּ֥וֹן הַבְּאֶֽרֹתִ֖י מִבְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן כִּ֚י גַּם־בְּאֵר֔וֹת תֵּחָשֵׁ֖ב עַל־בִּנְיָמִֽן׃
records.gloss: And two men, commanders of raiding bands, were [to the] son of Saul; [the] name of the one [was] Baanah, and [the] name of the second [was] Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from [the] sons of Benjamin; for also Beeroth is reckoned to Benjamin.
pieces: Saul's son had two men who were commanders of raiding bands. One was called Baanah and the other Rechab, and both were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the tribe of Benjamin, since Beeroth also is counted as part of Benjamin.

L.2: And Saul's son had two men, commanders of raiding bands; the name of the one [was] Baanah, and the name of the second [was] Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the sons of Benjamin; for Beeroth too is counted as [part of] Benjamin.

R.2: Ish-bosheth had two commanders of raiding parties. Their names were Baanah and Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from the town of Beeroth, in the tribe of Benjamin. (Beeroth is counted as part of Benjamin.)

decisions.choice: commanders of raiding bands: leaders of small fighting troops that made raids
decisions.reason: A *gedud* is a band of fighters sent out on raids (1 Samuel 30:8, 15; 2 Samuel 3:22). These two men led such bands in the service of Ish-bosheth.

decisions.choice: Beeroth: one of the Gibeonite towns, counted as part of Benjamin
decisions.reason: Beeroth was one of the four towns of the Gibeonites who made peace with Joshua (Joshua 9:17), and it was given to Benjamin (Joshua 18:25). The note makes clear that the two killers were Benjaminites, of Saul's own tribe, so the king's murderers came from his own people.

decisions.choice: commanders
decisions.reason: A *sar* in a military setting is a "commander" at every level. Readable says "raiding parties" for "raiding bands".

decisions.choice: the note about Beeroth in parentheses; Ish-bosheth named
decisions.reason: Readable sets the explanation about Beeroth apart, since it is a note by the writer, and names Saul's son as in verse 1.

records.source: וַיִּבְרְח֥וּ הַבְּאֵרֹתִ֖ים גִּתָּ֑יְמָה וַֽיִּהְיוּ־שָׁ֣ם גָּרִ֔ים עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And fled the Beerothites to Gittaim, and they have been there sojourning until the day the this.
pieces: The Beerothites had fled to Gittaim, and they have lived there as outsiders to this day.

L.3: And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there to this day.

R.3: The people of Beeroth had run away to Gittaim. They have lived there as outsiders to this day.

decisions.choice: the Beerothites had fled: background told from an earlier time
alternatives: the Beerothites fled at the time of the events of this chapter
decisions.reason: The verse explains why men of Beeroth were living elsewhere. When they fled is not said. It may have been when Saul attacked the Gibeonites (21:1-2), or when the Philistines took the land after Saul's defeat (1 Samuel 31:7).

decisions.choice: living as sojourners: residing as outsiders without the rights of the town's own people
decisions.reason: A *ger* lived among a people not his own, without a share of the land. Gittaim is named among the towns of Benjamin after the exile (Nehemiah 11:33).

decisions.choice: to this day: until the time of the writer
decisions.reason: "This day" is the writer's own day, not the time of the story. It shows the account was written down some time after the events.

decisions.choice: sojourners (Literal); outsiders (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: *Ger* is "sojourner" at Literal and "outsider" at Balanced and Readable, as elsewhere. Balanced and Readable say "had fled" because the flight came before the story.

records.source: וְלִיהֽוֹנָתָן֙ בֶּן־שָׁא֔וּל בֵּ֖ן נְכֵ֣ה רַגְלָ֑יִם בֶּן־חָמֵ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֣ים הָיָ֡ה בְּבֹ֣א שְׁמֻעַת֩ שָׁא֨וּל וִיהֽוֹנָתָ֜ן מִֽיִּזְרְעֶ֗אל וַתִּשָּׂאֵ֤הוּ אֹֽמַנְתּוֹ֙ וַתָּנֹ֔ס וַיְהִ֞י בְּחָפְזָ֥הּ לָנ֛וּס וַיִּפֹּ֥ל וַיִּפָּסֵ֖חַ וּשְׁמ֥וֹ מְפִיבֹֽשֶׁת׃
records.gloss: And to Jonathan son of Saul [was] a son stricken of feet; a son of five years he was in [the] coming of [the] report of Saul and Jonathan from Jezreel, and lifted him his nurse and fled; and it was in her hurrying to flee, and he fell and became lame; and his name [was] Mephibosheth.
pieces: (Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in both feet. He was five years old when word about Saul and Jonathan arrived from Jezreel. His nurse took him up and fled, but in her haste to get away he fell and was crippled. His name was Mephibosheth.)

L.4: (And Jonathan the son of Saul had a son crippled in [the] feet. He was five years old when the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse picked him up and fled; and as she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. And his name [was] Mephibosheth.)

R.4: (Saul's son Jonathan had a son whose feet were crippled. He was five years old when the news came from Jezreel that Saul and Jonathan had been killed. His nurse picked him up and ran away. But as she hurried to escape, he fell, and after that he could not walk properly. His name was Mephibosheth.)

decisions.choice: the verse is an aside that interrupts the story
alternatives: the verse explains why the murderers chose to kill Ish-bosheth and not another heir
decisions.reason: The story of Ish-bosheth's death stops for a note about Jonathan's son, then goes on in verse 5. The note shows that once Ish-bosheth was gone, the only one left of Saul's line through Jonathan was a lame boy, who could not lead an army or claim the throne. It also prepares for David's kindness to him (9:1-13).

decisions.choice: the report from Jezreel: the news of Saul's and Jonathan's death
decisions.reason: Israel had camped by the spring in Jezreel before the battle on Mount Gilboa, where Saul and Jonathan died (1 Samuel 29:1; 31:1-6). The household fled when the news came, fearing the Philistines or a rival for the throne.

decisions.choice: stricken of feet ... became lame: crippled in both feet from the fall
decisions.reason: The words for "feet" are dual, "both feet". The same description returns in 9:3, 13 and 19:27.

decisions.choice: Mephibosheth: called Merib-baal in Chronicles
decisions.reason: 1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40 call Jonathan's son Merib-baal. As with Ish-bosheth (see 2:8), Samuel puts "bosheth", "shame", in place of "baal".

decisions.choice: parentheses around the whole verse
decisions.reason: Every level sets the aside in parentheses so that the reader sees the story pause and then resume in verse 5.

decisions.choice: the news ... that Saul and Jonathan had been killed
decisions.reason: Readable says what the news was, which the Hebrew leaves to the reader of 1 Samuel 31.

records.source: וַיֵּ֨לְכ֜וּ בְּנֵֽי־רִמּ֤וֹן הַבְּאֵֽרֹתִי֙ רֵכָ֣ב וּבַעֲנָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ כְּחֹ֣ם הַיּ֔וֹם אֶל־בֵּ֖ית אִ֣ישׁ בֹּ֑שֶׁת וְה֣וּא שֹׁכֵ֔ב אֵ֖ת מִשְׁכַּ֥ב הַֽצָּהֳרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And went [the] sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, and came in [the] heat of the day to [the] house of Ish-bosheth, and he [was] lying [the] lying of the noon.
pieces: Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went off and reached Ish-bosheth's house in the heat of the day, while he was taking his midday rest.

L.5: And the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, went and came in the heat of the day to the house of Ish-bosheth, while he was lying down [for] the noon rest.

R.5: Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, set out for Ish-bosheth's house. They got there in the hottest part of the day, when he was lying down for his rest at noon.

decisions.choice: the noon rest: the usual time to lie down in the heat
decisions.reason: People rested through the hottest hours (Genesis 18:1). The house would be quiet and the king off guard.

decisions.choice: Ish-bosheth: Saul's son, made king by Abner
decisions.reason: The name is written as two words here. On the name and its form Eshbaal, see 2:8.

decisions.choice: taking his midday rest (Balanced); lying down for his rest at noon (Readable)
decisions.reason: Hebrew says "lying the lying of noon". Balanced and Readable say it once in plain words.

records.source: וְ֠הֵנָּה בָּ֜אוּ עַד־תּ֤וֹךְ הַבַּ֨יִת֙ לֹקְחֵ֣י חִטִּ֔ים וַיַּכֻּ֖הוּ אֶל־הַחֹ֑מֶשׁ וְרֵכָ֛ב וּבַעֲנָ֥ה אָחִ֖יו נִמְלָֽטוּ׃
records.gloss: And there they came into [the] middle of the house, taking wheat, and struck him into the belly; and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.
pieces: They came into the inner part of the house as though to fetch wheat, and they stabbed him in the belly. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah escaped.

L.6: And they came there into the middle of the house, fetching wheat, and they struck him in the belly; and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.

R.6: They went into the house as if they had come to get some wheat. They stabbed Ish-bosheth in the stomach, and then Rechab and his brother Baanah got away.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew is followed; the ancient Greek translation tells this verse differently
alternatives: the doorkeeper was cleaning wheat and fell asleep, and the brothers slipped in (ancient Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation reads, "And look, the doorkeeper of the house was cleaning wheat, and she grew drowsy and slept; and Rechab and Baanah the brothers slipped in." That reading explains how the men got past the door and does not tell the killing twice. The Hebrew is harder: it says the men came in "taking wheat" and struck him, and verse 7 then tells the killing again. Reviewers should check the Greek wording.

decisions.choice: taking wheat: probably a pretext for entering the house
alternatives: they went in to where the wheat was kept
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has only a participle, "taking wheat". It most likely means the men came in as if to collect wheat, perhaps rations for their troops, and so drew no notice. It may simply say where in the house they went, to the place where grain was kept.

decisions.choice: in the belly: the same wound that killed Asahel and Abner
decisions.reason: Abner struck Asahel in the belly (2:23), and Joab struck Abner in the same place (3:27). The third killing of the war comes the same way.

decisions.choice: as though to fetch wheat (Balanced); as if they had come to get some wheat (Readable); stabbed
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the pretext reading explicit, and say "stabbed" for "struck" since the wound was in the belly. This goes a little beyond the bare participle.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ הַבַּ֗יִת וְהֽוּא־שֹׁכֵ֤ב עַל־מִטָּתוֹ֙ בַּחֲדַ֣ר מִשְׁכָּב֔וֹ וַיַּכֻּ֨הוּ֙ וַיְמִתֻ֔הוּ וַיָּסִ֖ירוּ אֶת־רֹאשׁ֑וֹ וַיִּקְחוּ֙ אֶת־רֹאשׁ֔וֹ וַיֵּֽלְכ֛וּ דֶּ֥רֶךְ הָעֲרָבָ֖ה כָּל־הַלָּֽיְלָה׃
records.gloss: And they came [into] the house, and he [was] lying on his bed in [the] chamber of his lying, and they struck him and killed him and removed his head; and they took his head and went [the] way of the Arabah all the night.
pieces: They had entered the house while he lay on his bed in his bedroom, and they struck him down, killed him, and cut off his head. Taking the head with them, they traveled all night by the road through the Arabah.

L.7: And they came into the house while he was lying on his bed in his bedchamber, and they struck him and killed him and removed his head; and they took his head and went [by the] way of the Arabah all the night.

R.7: They had come into the house while Ish-bosheth was lying on his bed in his bedroom. They attacked him and killed him, and they cut off his head. Then they took the head and traveled all night along the road through the Jordan Valley.

decisions.choice: the verse goes back over the killing and tells it more fully
decisions.reason: Verse 6 gave the deed in brief; verse 7 returns to the moment they came in and adds where he lay, that they cut off his head, and how they left. Hebrew stories often tell an event first in short and then in full.

decisions.choice: they cut off his head: to carry proof of the king's death
decisions.reason: A head was taken as proof that an enemy was dead (1 Samuel 17:51, 54; 31:9). The men meant to show it to David and claim a reward.

decisions.choice: the way of the Arabah: the road down the Jordan Valley
decisions.reason: The Arabah is the deep valley of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Ish-bosheth's capital was Mahanaim, east of the Jordan (2:8, 12, 29). The men followed the valley south through the night before climbing to Hebron.

decisions.choice: bedroom; cut off his head; the Jordan Valley (Readable)
decisions.reason: "The chamber of his lying" is his bedroom, and "removed his head" means cut it off. Readable explains the Arabah as the Jordan Valley. Balanced and Readable say "had entered" because the verse looks back to verse 6.

records.source: וַ֠יָּבִאוּ אֶת־רֹ֨אשׁ אִֽישׁ־בֹּ֥שֶׁת אֶל־דָּוִד֮ חֶבְרוֹן֒ וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הִנֵּֽה־רֹ֣אשׁ אִֽישׁ־בֹּ֗שֶׁת בֶּן־שָׁאוּל֙ אֹֽיִבְךָ֔ אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּקֵּ֖שׁ אֶת־נַפְשֶׁ֑ךָ וַיִּתֵּ֣ן יְ֠הוָה לַֽאדֹנִ֨י הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ נְקָמוֹת֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה מִשָּׁא֖וּל וּמִזַּרְעֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: And they brought [the] head of Ish-bosheth to David [at] Hebron and said to the king, Here [is the] head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life; and has given Yahweh to my lord the king vengeance this day from Saul and from his offspring.
pieces: They brought Ish-bosheth's head to David at Hebron and told the king, "Look, here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, the one who sought your life. This day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given my lord the king vengeance on Saul and his descendants."

L.8: And they brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David [at] Hebron and said to the king, "Look, the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life! And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given my lord the king vengeance this day on Saul and on his offspring."

R.8: They brought the head to David at Hebron and said to him, "Look! This is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy who tried to kill you. Today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has paid back Saul and his family for you, my lord the king."

decisions.choice: your enemy, who sought your life: it may be Ish-bosheth or Saul
alternatives: Saul, your enemy, who sought your life
decisions.reason: The words can describe Ish-bosheth or his father. It was Saul who hunted David to kill him (1 Samuel 20:1; 23:15; 25:29), and the men's last words name Saul. The ambiguity is kept.

decisions.choice: Yahweh has given vengeance: the murderers claim God's approval for their deed
decisions.reason: They present the murder as Yahweh's justice on Saul's house for wronging David. David will answer with an oath in Yahweh's name that Yahweh, not they, rescued him (verse 9), and he refuses their claim.

decisions.choice: vengeance from Saul and his offspring: full payment for what Saul's house did
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is plural, "vengeances", which stresses that the score is settled completely. "Offspring" (literally "seed") means Saul's descendants and his royal line.

decisions.choice: has paid back Saul and his family for you
decisions.reason: Readable says what "given vengeance" means: Yahweh has repaid Saul's house on David's behalf.

records.source: וַיַּ֨עַן דָּוִ֜ד אֶת־רֵכָ֣ב׀וְאֶת־בַּעֲנָ֣ה אָחִ֗יו בְּנֵ֛י רִמּ֥וֹן הַבְּאֵֽרֹתִ֖י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֑ם חַי־יְהוָ֕ה אֲשֶׁר־פָּדָ֥ה אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֖י מִכָּל־צָרָֽה׃
records.gloss: And answered David Rechab and Baanah his brother, [the] sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, [As] lives Yahweh, who has ransomed my life from all distress,
pieces: David replied to Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble,

L.9: And David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, who has ransomed my life from all distress,

R.9: But David gave his answer to Rechab and his brother Baanah, Rimmon's sons from Beeroth. He told them, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has rescued me from every trouble. I give you my solemn word, as surely as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: David calls on the living God as witness to what he will say and do (1 Samuel 14:39). The oath governs the whole speech to the end of verse 11.

decisions.choice: who has ransomed my life from all distress: Yahweh, not these men, has saved David
decisions.reason: The verb means to set free, as by paying a price. David will give the same oath on his deathbed (1 Kings 1:29). He answers their claim in verse 8: Yahweh has always rescued him and needs no murder to do it.

decisions.choice: rescued; every trouble
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "rescued" for "ransomed", the plain sense here, and "as surely as ... lives" for the bare oath.

decisions.choice: two sentences, with "I give you my solemn word" supplied
decisions.reason: Readable puts the description of Yahweh first and states the oath as a sentence of its own, so that the long sentence of verses 9-11 can be broken into short ones.

records.heading: David punishes the murderers

records.source: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה־מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא־הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי־ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה׃
records.gloss: for the [one] telling to me, saying, Look, has died Saul, and he was like [one] bringing good news in his eyes, and I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, which [was] to give to him [for] news;
pieces: when the man who told me, 'Look, Saul is dead,' thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and put him to death in Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news,

L.10: when the one telling me, saying, 'Look, Saul is dead,' was in his own eyes like one bringing good news, I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, which [was] my giving to him [a reward for] news,

R.10: Once a man came to me and said, 'Saul is dead.' He thought he was bringing me good news. But I seized him and put him to death in Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news.

decisions.choice: the man who told David of Saul's death at Ziklag
decisions.reason: The Amalekite came to Ziklag with Saul's crown and claimed to have killed him, expecting thanks; David had him put to death (1:1-16). David now holds the two brothers to the same standard.

decisions.choice: in his own eyes: as he himself thought
decisions.reason: The man saw himself as a bearer of good news. The verb is the one used for bringing welcome news of a victory (1 Samuel 31:9).

decisions.choice: which was my giving him for news: that was his reward
alternatives: the one to whom I should have given a reward for his news
decisions.reason: The words are bitter: the reward he looked for was his death. The noun for "news" can also mean the reward given for good news.

decisions.choice: put him to death; That was the reward I gave him
decisions.reason: Balanced makes the irony plain with "reward" and keeps the sentence open into verse 11. In 1:15 David had another man carry out the killing, so "put to death" is used.

decisions.choice: the story told in short sentences
decisions.reason: Readable tells the earlier event as a short story of its own, then draws the lesson in verse 11.

records.source: אַ֞ף כִּֽי־אֲנָשִׁ֣ים רְשָׁעִ֗ים הָרְג֧וּ אֶת־אִישׁ־צַדִּ֛יק בְּבֵית֖וֹ עַל־מִשְׁכָּב֑וֹ וְעַתָּ֗ה הֲל֨וֹא אֲבַקֵּ֤שׁ אֶת־דָּמוֹ֙ מִיֶּדְכֶ֔ם וּבִעַרְתִּ֥י אֶתְכֶ֖ם מִן־הָאָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: how much more when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his house on his bed! And now, shall I not require his blood from your hand and remove you from the earth?
pieces: how much more when wicked men have killed an innocent man in his own house on his bed! Now then, shall I not demand his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth?"

L.11: how much more when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed! And now, shall I not require his blood from your hand and purge you from the earth?"

R.11: You are wicked men, and you have killed an innocent man in his own house, on his own bed. That is far worse! So now I will hold you responsible for his death, and I will wipe you off the earth."

decisions.choice: how much more: an argument from the lesser to the greater
decisions.reason: If David killed a man who only brought news of a death in battle, he must punish far more those who murdered a man in his sleep.

decisions.choice: a righteous man: one innocent of any crime that deserved death
decisions.reason: *Tsaddiq* here describes Ish-bosheth's standing in this matter: he had done nothing to deserve being killed. It is not a claim about his whole life. The "wicked men" are those guilty of the crime.

decisions.choice: require his blood from your hand: hold you to account for his death
decisions.reason: To "require blood" is to demand the life of a murderer for the life he took (Genesis 9:5-6; 42:22). "Remove" (literally "burn out" or "purge") is the word of the laws that remove evil from Israel (Deuteronomy 19:13, 19; 21:21).

decisions.choice: innocent man
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "innocent" because "righteous" might suggest a claim about his goodness in general. Literal keeps "righteous".

decisions.choice: the question becomes a statement
decisions.reason: Readable turns David's question, which expects the answer yes, into a firm statement, and states the comparison as "That is far worse".

records.source: וַיְצַו֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת־הַנְּעָרִ֜ים וַיַּהַרְג֗וּם וַֽיְקַצְּצ֤וּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם֙ וְאֶת־רַגְלֵיהֶ֔ם וַיִּתְל֥וּ עַל־הַבְּרֵכָ֖ה בְּחֶבְר֑וֹן וְאֵ֨ת רֹ֤אשׁ אִֽישׁ־בֹּ֨שֶׁת֙ לָקָ֔חוּ וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ בְקֶֽבֶר־אַבְנֵ֖ר בְּחֶבְרֽוֹן׃פ
records.gloss: And commanded David the young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and their feet and hanged [them] by the pool in Hebron; and [the] head of Ish-bosheth they took and buried in [the] tomb of Abner in Hebron.
pieces: Then David gave orders to his young men, and they killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies beside the pool in Hebron. But Ish-bosheth's head they took and buried in Abner's tomb at Hebron.

L.12: And David commanded the young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and their feet and hanged [them] beside the pool in Hebron; and they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried [it] in the tomb of Abner in Hebron.

R.12: Then David gave orders to his soldiers, and they put the two men to death. They cut off their hands and feet and hung up their bodies beside the pool in Hebron, where everyone could see them. But they took Ish-bosheth's head and buried it in Abner's tomb in Hebron.

decisions.choice: the young men: David's fighting men
decisions.reason: *Ne'arim* can mean servants or young soldiers; here they act on the king's orders, as in 2:14 and 1:15.

decisions.choice: cut off their hands and feet and hanged them: a public mark of disgrace
alternatives: the hands and feet were cut off only to disgrace the bodies
decisions.reason: Hanging a body in public showed that the dead man had been put under a curse and served as a warning (Deuteronomy 21:22-23; Joshua 10:26). Cutting off the hands that did the killing and the feet that ran with the head may have marked the crime. Hebron's pool was a public place, so all who came would see that David had no part in the murder.

decisions.choice: buried in Abner's tomb: an honorable burial
decisions.reason: Abner had been buried at Hebron with David mourning him (3:31-32). Ish-bosheth's head was laid with the man who had made him king.

decisions.choice: his young men; his soldiers (Readable); their bodies; where everyone could see them (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose men these were and that the bodies were hung. Readable names the young men as soldiers and adds that the bodies were on public view, which the place and the custom imply.
